planting.note: Direct sow in fall in dry-mesic, well-drained upland soil in full sun to light shade; winter cold exposure improves spring germination and mimics the woodland-edge conditions this species favors.

directions: Broadleaf ironweed grows wild along the Appalachian chain from Pennsylvania south to Alabama, favoring open woodlands, cleared forest edges, and dry roadside banks rather than the wet bottomlands preferred by many of its ironweed relatives. Wide, oblanceolate leaves and an upright, wand-like stem carry tight clusters of bright reddish-purple flower heads from late summer into mid-fall. Because it comes from dry-mesic upland sites, it tolerates lean, well-drained soil and light shade better than most Vernonia and rarely needs supplemental watering once rooted in. The late bloom period draws heavy butterfly and native bee traffic just as many other prairie nectar sources are fading.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in average to dry, well-drained upland soil in full sun; this species is virtually unknown in the nursery trade, so seed from wild-collected or botanic garden sources is the most reliable start.

directions: Native to the upland deciduous forests of Tennessee, Georgia, and Alabama, this little-grown ironweed is easy to tell apart from its relatives by its sunken, wrinkled leaf veins and smooth, waxy stems that shade from maroon to smoky purple through the growing season. Clusters of purple composite flowers open in late summer and fall on stems that stay disease-free but can flop over without some support from nearby planting or a light stake, a known weak point of the species. Grow it in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun, where it holds up better than in richer, moister ground. Its late nectar draws butterflies and bees at a time when few other woodland-edge perennials are still flowering.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Set out nursery divisions or container plants in spring after frost danger has passed, in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this Plant Delights Nursery selection forms an unusually tight, ball-shaped mound compared with other narrowleaf ironweed cultivars.

directions: Late Night forms a dense, rounded, almost globe-shaped mound of fine, needle-thin foliage that holds its shape without shearing, then covers itself in hundreds of small bright purple-violet flowers in late summer, drawing hummingbirds along with the usual bees and butterflies. Selected from wild narrowleaf ironweed populations found on Arkansas and Oklahoma rock outcrops, it inherits that ancestry's tolerance for lean, rocky, fast-draining soil and needs no staking despite its multi-branched, floriferous habit. Plant in full sun in average to lean soil; once established it shrugs off heat and drought far better than most border perennials. Cut the old growth back in late winter before new shoots emerge.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out nursery divisions or container plants in spring after frost danger has passed, in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Violet Night is a Walters Gardens hybrid of coastalplain and narrowleaf ironweed bred for a dense, upright clump rather than the sprawling habit of either parent.

directions: Bred by Hans Hansen at Walters Gardens from a cross of coastalplain ironweed and narrowleaf ironweed, Violet Night was the breeding program's first ironweed introduction and produces a dense, upright clump topped with abundant clusters of rich purple flowers starting in midsummer, noticeably earlier than many ironweed cultivars. The flowers draw an especially heavy and varied pollinator crowd, from bumblebees to swallowtails, through the peak of the growing season. Plant in full sun in average to moist, well-drained soil, where its sturdy stems stand upright without staking despite the plant's substantial four-foot size. It needs little more than a late-winter cutback once established and tolerates both average garden moisture and brief dry spells.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall on the surface of damp to seasonally wet, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; seeds benefit from winter moisture and cold exposure before germinating in spring.

directions: Ragged thoroughwort takes its name from the coarse, irregular teeth along the margins of its narrow, oblong leaves, a feature that distinguishes it from the closely related roundleaf thoroughwort. It grows naturally in damp, sandy soils of longleaf pine savannas, bogs, and other seasonally wet lowlands from Massachusetts south to peninsular Florida and west into Kentucky, Tennessee, and Mississippi, though it occasionally turns up in surprisingly dry, mesic woodland edges as well. Small, fuzzy white flower heads with no showy ray petals cluster at the branch tips from August into October, offering a modest but reliable nectar source for late-season pollinators. Keep the soil consistently damp to wet in full sun to light shade, mimicking the seasonally saturated habitats where it thrives in the wild.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, well-drained floodplain or bottomland soil in partial shade to full sun; this rhizomatous species slowly forms colonies once established.

directions: Smallflower thoroughwort spreads by short rhizomes into loose colonies of upright stems that branch mainly near the tips, topped from late July through October by a profusion of tiny white flower heads made up entirely of disc florets, with no ray florets to give them a showy edge. It occurs naturally in well-drained floodplain forests, bottomland terrace woodlands, wet flatwoods, and roadside ditches across the coastal plain from Maryland to Texas, reaching inland into Missouri and Kentucky. It is easily confused with the similar Eupatorium linearifolium but has smaller flower heads and a distinctly upper-branching stem structure. Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and expect it to slowly widen into a colony rather than stay a tight clump.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database
Digital Atlas of the Virginia Flora

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, acidic sandy soil in full sun; this species is rare and vulnerable in the wild, so seed should come only from cultivated or ethically sourced stock, never wild-collected populations.

directions: Pine barren boneset is a regionally rare wetland perennial with a disjunct native range centered on the New Jersey Pine Barrens and scattered acidic bogs and wet savannas in the Carolinas, having already disappeared from historic populations in New York and Delaware. The whole plant is noticeably glandular and sticky-pubescent, a trait that sets it apart from most other white-flowered Eupatorium species, and it carries flat-topped clusters of small white flower heads, each with seven to eleven disc florets and no rays, above a flat-topped, roughly waist-high frame. It requires constantly moist to wet, acidic, sandy soil in full sun, closely mimicking the seepage bogs and pine barren wetlands where it survives in the wild. Because NatureServe lists it as vulnerable, gardeners growing it are effectively contributing to ex-situ conservation of the species.
sources: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in spring; 'Album' is a white-flowered sport of blue mistflower that self-seeds readily and can be shared or moved easily as small divisions.

directions: 'Album' is a pure white-flowered form of blue mistflower, standing out sharply from the species' usual powder-blue to violet color while keeping the same frothy, ageratum-like flower clusters from August into October. Its habit is narrower and more upright than the wild species, staying only 8 to 16 inches wide even as it reaches 3 to 4 feet tall, and it has earned recognition from both the Royal Horticultural Society and the Missouri Botanical Garden for its garden merit. Grow it in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil, and expect it to self-sow modestly around the original clump over time. It draws the same strong late-season crowd of migrating monarchs and native bees as its blue counterpart, making it a useful color echo in a white-and-blue fall pollinator planting.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Award of Merit records
